written-input: Ian Weisberger, CoinRoutes Inc Letter To SEC and CFTC
key-points: The letter emphasizes that digital asset markets involve transactions between spot commodities and securities, necessitating a novel regulatory framework distinct from traditional finance. CoinRoutes warns that imposing traditional market regulations (e.g., tick size, fee caps) on crypto markets could increase trading costs and reduce competitiveness, potentially pushing liquidity to less regulated international venues. Effective monitoring of manipulative behaviors like momentum ignition requires integrated surveillance across both spot and derivative crypto markets—something not currently achieved in traditional equity markets.
text:
To: Chair Paul Atkins, SEC
Interim Chair Caroline Pham, CFTC
From: Ian Weisberger, CEO Coinroutes & Co Founder
David Weisberger, Board Member - CoinRoutes
We are pleased to comment on several of the issues to be discussed at the upcoming Joint
SEC CFTC Roundtable on Regulatory Harmonization Efforts. While there are good reasons to
harmonize rules and coordinate efforts between the agencies in the oversight of interconnected
Futures and Equities markets, the need to regulate Digital Assets brings it to a new level. As
you are aware, there are crypto assets that are deemed to be commodities, there is a robust
swap/futures market on those assets and there will be assets deemed securities. As a result,
unlike traditional finance, there will be transactions between spot commodities and securities
that requires a new regulatory approach.
In addition, the crypto market structure has evolved without regulation, yet it functions extremely
well for institutional investors. Arguably, it has become an excellent laboratory for
understanding how markets would function in the absence of rules such as legislated tick sizes,
prohibitions on locked or crossed markets, trade through protection and fee caps.
At CoinRoutes, we have a unique perspective into the functioning of crypto spot and derivative
markets worldwide. Our firm, founded over 7 years ago, is a market leader in the provision of
algorithmic trading software having facilitated over $500 Billion in notional value traded, across
spot and derivative products. CoinRoutes processes multiple terabytes of market data every day
and connects to all the major US and international exchanges.
While many commenters will tell you the crypto markets are not “orderly” and are ripe for
manipulation, our data shows them to be very transparent with lower barriers to entry than either
futures or equity markets under Regulation NMS. In fact, our recent transaction cost analysis
(TCA) shows that institutional orders using our algorithms can be handled at much lower trading
costs than for similar sized orders in regulated markets. For example, in 2025, CoinRoutes
handled over $12 billion in unconstrained spot crypto comprising more than 3000 large
institutional orders with an aggregate total execution cost of under 5 basis points from the
aggregated “far” side of the market. This result, which compares quite favorably to NMS
institutional order slippage, was achieved, despite markets that are consistently crossed, without
any tick size constraints, or prudential regulators looking for market manipulation. In overseas
perpetual swap markets, CoinRoutes software executed over $65 billion across over 22,000
large, unconstrained, institutional orders at an average improvement of 1.7 basis points from the
“far” side of the market. Such performance would be impossible in the current US futures
markets where market makers have a virtual monopoly at trading inside of the spread.

As a result of this experience, we urge caution in considering “normalization” of regulation that
would result in higher crypto trading costs in the U.S. while helping overseas competitors. We
will go into more detail as we comment on three of the topics you plan to discuss in your
roundtable.
Promoting Fair and Orderly Markets
The bulk of our commentary is on this question, as CoinRoutes is in the business of helping our
clients execute at low cost, with low market impact in both spot and derivative markets.
Considering those markets best align with the SEC and CFTC respectively, we will discuss spot
in the context of securities regulation and the perpetual swap markets in the context of futures
regulation. In both sections we will start with a comparison of the market structures and then
share actual execution statistics for CoinRoutes clients.
Spot Market Market Structure, Compared to NMS Securities
There are three main differences between the crypto spot markets and equity markets under
Regulation NMS: zero intermarket regulation, no tick size regulation and no fee regulation.
The result of these differences is a market with no substantive queueing at price levels, many
more price level / market combinations and a requirement to consider fees in all routing
decisions, particularly as markets on a gross basis are almost always crossed.
1. Queuing - In the crypto market it is virtually unseen to have significant order size across
multiple orders at the same price at the same time. We have not calculated the
percentage of time recently, but it was less than 1/100th of 1 percent when we last
measured this and have no reason to believe it has changed as the tick sizes are so
small, relative to the price of the asset, that it is much cheaper to price improve than to
try and “race” orders to the exchange. The result is less emphasis on high frequency
trading based on speed and a more competitive market that has lower barriers to entry.
2. More Market Data - To illustrate this point, we used CoinRoutes book aggregation
service to determine how many individual price/exchange combinations were within 1%
of the midprice for Bitcoin, which, considering its volatility, is a reasonable proxy for what
trading algorithms might consider. On average, this number ranges between 500 to
1000 unique combinations per side of the order book. As a reference, standard equity
algorithms rarely look beyond 5 price levels in their decision making, so the difference is
substantial. From a regulatory perspective, this shows how the crypto markets have
much more order competition than equities, proving that Reg NMS is likely
counterproductive in its stated goal of increasing it.
3. Fees are unconstrained - To understand the magnitude of this, consider that the average
institutional fee for top clients in spot crypto is 2 basis points (0.02%). Considering the
tick size for Bitcoin, as the largest asset, is 1 cent ($.01), that means the lowest fees
charged, at todays price of $115,000, is $23, which is 2300 times the minimum tick. This
compares to equity markets where access fees are a fraction of the tick size and is why

markets always appear to be crossed, but when fees are taken into account are not. We
would suspect that market structure experts from the equity world would look at this
situation and declare it “messy” and hard to navigate. The results we have shown at
CoinRoutes, however, clearly disprove that assertion. As stated earlier, CoinRoutes
clients achieved excellent results as shown here:
Notice the chart shows three benchmarks, the far side, the midprice and the CoinRoutes cost
calculator. The far side shows lower slippage than the midprice, which is indicative of the fact
that the offer price, on average for these orders, was 0.8 basis points lower than the bid price on
a gross basis. Considering the size of these orders, it was also true that the average size
available on the bid or offer was a miniscule fraction of the order size. That is shown in the
outperformance of the cost calculator by over 65 basis points. That software uses the
instantaneous aggregated order book to create the benchmark and is a rough approximation of
what optimal smart routing would have achieved. To the extent that commenters point to the
available liquidity being too thin for institutional trading, this disproves that assertion.
It is also instructive to look at the distribution of the performance. In the aggregate, the average
slippage on an equal weighted basis was actually 3.66 basis points, while the standard
deviation was 90 basis points indicating the volatility of the market. That said, the following dot
plot shows consistent performance for the large majority of these institutional orders. This is
indicative of a market with high predictability, particularly with respect to the volatility of the
assets.

The point we are trying to make is not to extol the virtues of the CoinRoutes platform, however.
It simply demonstrates, with modern technology, the market can adapt to a market structure
deemed chaotic and unruly. It also shows, there is potentially a real risk of liquidity fleeing the
U.S. if it becomes much cheaper to trade on markets that are not subject to over-regulation.
Perpetual Swap Market Structure, Compared to Listed Futures
The main difference between the CFTC regulated futures markets and the perpetual swap
markets overseas is direct client access. All the markets have tick sizes set by the exchanges
and all are single counterparty markets insofar as it is very hard to manage margin across
platforms. The perpetual swap exchanges, in general, do have smaller tick sizes, however and
by allowing clients to connect directly, have more order competition. To put this in perspective,
the average tick size for Bitcoin perpetual swaps is 10 cents, and that is, quite often the spread
observed in each market. At the same time the tick size for the CME Bitcoin future is 5 dollars
or 50 times higher, with observed spreads often much larger, albeit for much larger size.
Putting this tick size difference in perspective, here is a chart of CoinRoutes client performance
for institutional sized orders on perpetual swap exchanges:

Notice that the performance vs the Far side shows more outperformance than vs the Mid price,
which is due to the fact that the bid is always below the offer price on the individual exchange
used. That said, the 1.7 basis points of outperformance is particularly important to
contextualize as the average spread is much lower than for CME products. The larger
outperformance of 6.5 basis points vs the cost calculator is indicative of the liquidity on the
perpetual swap markets compared to spot, where the performance was roughly ten times
higher. This leads to the conclusion that the perpetual swap market structure is extremely
efficient and provides a valuable service to those firms looking for low cost hedging or
speculation.
As with spot, we looked at the distribution of this performance as well. In the swap market, the
average, unweighted, order showed a slippage of under 2 basis points and the standard
deviation of performance was roughly 25 basis points. This consistency is shown in the
following dot plot that shows more outliers with positive performance driving the weighted
outperformance:

Public Dissemination of Trade Data
While it may not always be as it is today, the crypto markets are more transparent than
traditional markets. Crypto exchanges publish their full order books and trade feeds for free,
while on-chain data provides much more insight into large movements than traditional SEC filing
data. In response to the lack of “official” consolidated data, many companies, including
CoinRoutes, have created their own consolidation, while a number of firms take the publicly
available data to do the same thing. If the SEC or CFTC contemplated the creation of a
consolidated tape, however, it is important to point out how important fees and disparate tick
sizes would complicate that endeavor. Due to those factors, different firms with different fee
tiers at various exchanges would see the same data differently. That would limit the utility of
such a feed for the average investor, while the existence of numerous free sources of data
make it unnecessary.
It is also worth noting that supporting Best Execution reporting (Rule 605) was a major use of
consolidated data in the equity markets. Due to the differences between the markets noted
earlier, a consolidated tape would not be as useful in crypto, particularly since it would not likely
be superior to any of the public sources of data. At the same time, firms such as CoinRoutes
produce our own best execution reporting and the public data available would allow the leading
firms in the space to do so broadly.
Monitoring of Underlying Markets
There is certainly scope for improved monitoring of crypto markets, particularly for manipulative
behaviors such as “momentum ignition” as well as surveillance of potential conflicts of interest.

Such monitoring could improve investor confidence in the market, which would improve liquidity
and smooth out some of the volatility.
The key, however, to momentum ignition surveillance would be to aggregate the data of both
derivative and spot exchanges together, which does not exist today in the equity markets. The
reason this could be important is that the derivative markets have more liquidity, but those
markets and their participants use the spot price on reference exchanges for determining risk.
Thus, if an unscrupulous participant builds up a sizeable position long spot and short perpetual
swaps, for example, it is possible for them to profit by dumping the spot first, particularly during
illiquid periods, and then buying back the perpetual swaps after a wave of liquidations was
triggered. This past weekend, there was a Sunday night / Monday morning liquidation cascade
in the crypto markets that might have been the result of such a trading strategy. According to
coinglass.com
, over $1.6 Billion in notional value was liquidated, although it is worth pointing out
over 75% of the liquidations were in less liquid assets than Bitcoin. Were there coordinated
surveillance between the largest perpetual swap exchanges and spot markets, intentional
selloffs would likely be uncovered and participants would be more confident in the integrity of
the markets.
Conclusion: While there are many structural issues to work out over the long run as more
assets become tokenized, it is important to let innovation continue in the crypto markets
themselves. As more data becomes available to the regulators, we believe that it will become
readily apparent to the participants in legacy financial markets that the current regulatory
environment is overly prescriptive. As a result, we would suggest caution on how to regulate
the digital asset markets in the U.S., by focussing on issues such as market integrity via
surveillance and promoting the concept of best execution.

written-input: Epistria, LLC - When Digital Evidence of “Nothing Happened” Isn’t Good Enough When Digital Evidence of “Nothing Happened” Isn’t Good Enough
key-points: Courts lack clear standards for evaluating digital evidence that purports to prove a negative (e.g., no access, no transaction), making such evidence vulnerable to challenge and potentially unreliable in litigation. As cryptographically generated “negative receipts” emerge, courts will need to assess them using technology-neutral criteria like authenticity, integrity, and chain of custody—while also developing new standards specific to negative proofs. Portable digital artifacts proving non-occurrence may be discoverable, raising concerns about privilege waiver and confidentiality, especially when such artifacts reveal internal systems or were not created under legal direction.
text:
1
When Digital Evidence of “Nothing Happened”
Isn’t Good Enough
By C.S. Thomas, Epistria, LLC
Law360 recently reported a Nevada trust’s allegation that Texas firms promised cryptocurrency trades,
delivered none, and now cannot account for $9 million. (Nevada Trust Accuses Texas Firms Of $9M
Crypto Scheme) Whatever the merits, the pleading posture is familiar: a party asserts that what should
have happened did not—no delivery, no trades, no movement of assets.
Our systems are surprisingly poor at proving non-occurrence. We can authenticate affirmative events (a
signed contract, a posted ledger entry, a confirmed transfer). But when the issue is a negative—no path,
no access, no trade—digital evidence typically devolves to log searches, screenshots, and testimony.
“No row found” is not a legal standard.
The real gap: affirmative proof of absence
Modern enterprises record nearly everything, except the most contested category of all: the things that
did not happen. In disputes, that gap plays out in three recurring questions:
♦ Was the missing record the result of no event, or bad recordkeeping (or intentional deletion)?
♦ Does “we looked and didn’t see it” amount to anything more than assurance?
♦ How can a court distinguish true non-occurrence from after-the-fact reconstruction?
The UK’s Post Office/Horizon scandal is the cautionary tale. For years, prosecutions relied on software
outputs that were later shown to be error-prone; thousands of sub-postmasters were wrongly accused or
convicted. The public inquiry concluded the Post Office “maintained the fiction” that the system was
reliable, and the justice system accepted digital outputs without adequate scrutiny—an institutional
failure now described as one of Britain’s largest miscarriages of justice. The common thread is
evidentiary: courts accepted what the system said happened, while those accused struggled to show
what didn’t. (https://www.ft.com/content/0695206e-60f8-4565-a46f-c7158639f61c)

2
Lawyers have seen this movie before: novel tech can be
domesticated
There is precedent for incorporating new forms of digital proof. In England and Wales, the judiciary
and law reform bodies moved deliberately to recognize cryptoassets and smart contracts, laying
groundwork for the admissibility and treatment of associated records. The UK Jurisdiction Taskforce
issued a landmark legal statement in 2019, followed by judicial uptake (e.g., AA v Persons Unknown,
confirming Bitcoin as property and supporting proprietary remedies)—a measured, doctrine-first path
that normalized what had been “novel” technology. That is a template for how the bar can domesticate
unfamiliar evidence without over- or under-reacting.
(https://www.judiciary.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/LegalStatementLaunch.GV_.2-1.pdf)
At the European level, guidance on electronic evidence has likewise emphasized technology-neutral
admissibility: courts should accept any technique that can demonstrate authenticity, accuracy, and
integrity—without giving automatic preference or distrust to a specific technology. That stance is the
right starting point for evaluating emerging forms of provable negatives.
(https://rm.coe.int/guidelines-on-electronic-evidence-and-explanatory-memorandum/1680968ab5)
Why this matters beyond one crypto dispute
Across regulated sectors, proving a negative is becoming outcome-determinative:
♦ Financial services: establishing that no unauthorized path existed from account A to B can allocate or
avoid liability.
♦ Healthcare & privacy: demonstrating that data did not cross a jurisdictional boundary can decide a
GDPR investigation. (EU data-transfer supervision already pressures organizations to substantiate
cross-border non-events with more than policy statements.)
(https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2023-05/final_for_issue_ov_transfers_decision_12-05-
23.pdf)
♦ Supply chains & SBOMs: showing that a banned vendor or vulnerable component never entered the
dependency tree is as important as showing approved ones did.

3
If courts and agencies continue to rely on mutable logs and attestations for negatives, we invite more
Nevada-style fights—and more Horizon-style miscarriages.
Two issues the bar should get ahead of: reliability and
privilege
Reliability/admissibility. When parties begin offering cryptographically generated denials—portable
evidence purporting to show that, at a given time, no path/no access/no transaction existed—courts will
need standards. Technology-neutral principles already exist: authenticity, integrity, accuracy, chain-of-
custody. What’s missing are clear expectations for negative digital proofs (e.g., scope definitions, time
bounding, anchoring to independent references) and how they rank against logs and testimony.
Privilege/confidentiality. This is the sleeper issue for in-house counsel. “Negative receipts” may be
discoverable if they exist outside counsel’s direction. Even when prepared at counsel’s request,
portability cuts both ways: the same artifact that convinces a regulator can be compelled by an
opponent. Bar committees should address:
♦ When (if ever) generating portable negative proofs waives privilege or work product.
♦ How to structure retention and destruction policies for such artifacts.
♦ Whether regulators should (or should not) demand production of negative proofs as a matter of
course.
♦ How confidentiality orders should treat these artifacts when they unavoidably reveal aspects of
internal systems, policies, or identifiers.
A measured path forward
The playbook is not to bless any particular technology; it is to prepare a framework for whatever
emerges. The profession has already navigated similar inflection points — digital signatures, email
metadata, blockchain records — by articulating evaluation criteria first and adapting practice later.
Bar committees and professional associations might consider:
1. Technology-neutral guidance on how to evaluate evidence of non-occurrence — for example,
scoping definitions, time bounding, and criteria for reproducibility.

4
2. Privilege and discovery questions — when the creation of portable negative proofs could waive
privilege, and how protective orders might handle artifacts that inevitably reveal aspects of
internal systems.
3. Case-management practices — early judicial conferences to frame how negative evidence will
be handled, or burden-shifting protocols when only one party controls the relevant systems.
4. Coordination with regulators — exploring whether consistent expectations across agencies
would reduce uncertainty for companies facing parallel oversight.
The Nevada complaint is a reminder that “we checked and didn’t see it” is a fragile evidentiary model.
The Horizon inquiry shows the cost when institutions over-credit system outputs while leaving no
reliable way to prove absence. These measures may not prevent the next scandal, but it might reduce
the risk — and improve fairness — by beginning to examine how cryptographic proofs of non-
occurrence could be treated within established evidentiary standards.

written-input: Epistria, LLC - Crypto’s Evidentiary Debt Crisis Crypto’s Evidentiary Debt Crisis
key-points: Evidentiary asymmetry in crypto markets undermines enforcement because regulators cannot prove the absence of misconduct (e.g., wash trading, front-running), creating a persistent "evidentiary debt." Cryptographic receipts of absence offer a novel compliance mechanism by mathematically attesting that prohibited activities did not occur within a defined scope, enhancing auditability and legal defensibility. Mandating or endorsing such receipts would support the SEC’s goals of clear regulatory boundaries, tailored disclosures, and stronger investor protections through verifiable compliance.
text:
Crypto’s Evidentiary Debt Crisis
Problem Statement
Cryptocurrency markets face a unique evidentiary challenge. Investigations and enforcement actions
often fail not because misconduct cannot be observed, but because the absence of misconduct cannot be
proven. Regulators and exchanges alike are left with evidentiary debt—the unresolved burden of
proving negatives.
Key regulatory blind spots include:
♦ Demonstrating that no wash trading artificially inflated reported volumes.
♦ Establishing that no front-running occurred before major transactions.
♦ Confirming that no unauthorized wallet access compromised investor assets.
♦ Verifying that no off-book trades manipulated prices behind the scenes.
Current State of Practice
Today, crypto exchanges provide audit logs and transaction records that document what occurred.
These artifacts are inherently activity-focused; they cannot attest to what did not occur. As a result,
when challenged, neither regulators nor market participants can produce definitive evidence of absence.
This evidentiary gap undermines both enforcement and investor confidence.
Possible Solution: Cryptographic Receipts of Absence
Recent advances in compliance cryptography enable the generation of receipts that prove absence as
well as presence. These receipts can function as tamper-evident mathematical attestations that a
prohibited event did not take place within a defined scope and timeframe. In practice, they would allow
exchanges to produce verifiable proof that:
♦ No wash trades were executed.
♦ No front-running transactions were admitted to the ledger.
♦ No unauthorized wallet access took place.
♦ No hidden order book was maintained.
Alignment with SEC Task Force Priorities
This evidentiary capability directly supports the Task Force’s stated priorities:
♦ Clear regulatory lines — Cryptographic receipts provide bright-line separation between compliant
and non-compliant activity, moving beyond subjective policy interpretation.
♦ Tailored disclosure — Receipts of absence can be standardized as a disclosure framework, giving
investors assurance in domains where traditional reporting falls short.
♦ Investor protection — By supplying mathematical evidence that no manipulation occurred, receipts
strengthen confidence in market integrity and reduce litigation risk.
Case Example: Nevada Litigation
In a recent Nevada case, a trust alleged that $9 million in crypto trades never happened. Neither the
exchange nor the plaintiffs could prove presence or absence conclusively. This evidentiary stalemate
illustrates the systemic weakness: without cryptographic receipts of absence, disputes devolve into
unverifiable claims, eroding confidence in both markets and oversight.

Conclusion
The SEC’s Crypto Task Force has the opportunity to close a structural evidentiary gap in digital asset
regulation. By encouraging or requiring cryptographic proofs of absence as part of compliance and
disclosure frameworks, the Task Force can transform crypto oversight from a trust-based regime into a
verification-based one—reducing evidentiary debt, enhancing investor protection, and strengthening
the integrity of U.S. markets.

written-input: Gridtek LLC Subject: Recommendation on Governance for Private Blockchain Operations
key-points: Private blockchains operated by companies should be governed by internal corporate structures (e.g., boards), ensuring accountability and operational continuity. Coins used within private blockchains for governance and utility purposes should not be classified as securities if not offered to institutional investors or traded on public exchanges. Transparent transaction visibility on private blockchains can reduce the need for external regulatory oversight while maintaining stakeholder trust.
text:
Subject: Recommendation on Governance for Private Blockchain Operations
Dear Commissioners,
I hope this letter finds you well. On behalf of Gridtek, I would like to respectfully offer a
recommendation regarding the governance and regulatory treatment of private blockchains operated
by companies.
1. Governance Framework
We recommend that private companies adopt governance structures overseen by their board
members or equivalent governing bodies. This approach provides accountability, effective
succession planning, and continuity of access to the underlying technology, helping ensure
operational stability over time.
2. Commitment to Innovation
Gridtek has a strong interest in establishing governance structures that foster both stability and
innovation. By creating clear, transparent frameworks, private blockchains can serve as reliable
platforms that support technological advancement, encourage responsible growth, and sustain long-
term innovation.
3. Purpose of Coins
Coins issued on private blockchains should be designed primarily for governance, operational
functions, and utility within the ecosystem. Their role is to facilitate functionality and decision-making,
not to serve as investment instruments.
4. Transparency
All transactions on these blockchains should remain publicly visible. Transparency allows
stakeholders to maintain trust in the system while reducing the need for burdensome oversight.
5. Regulatory Considerations
We recommend that coins designed for governance and utility within private company blockchains
not be treated as traditional securities when they are not sold to institutional investors or listed on
public exchanges. Recognizing this distinction would provide clarity, reduce unnecessary burdens,
and encourage companies to innovate responsibly.
Conclusion
A framework that acknowledges the unique nature of private company-operated blockchains would
support innovation, ensure stability through structured governance, and maintain public trust through
transparent operations.
We appreciate your consideration of these recommendations and your ongoing efforts to balance

Letter of Presentation
September 21, 2025
To the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC),
It is with great respect that I submit the proposal entitled "IoT-Enabled Tokenization of Physical
Assets with Verifiable Physical Proof: A Comprehensive Regulatory and Technical
Framework." This document is accompanied by the following appendices, which form an integral
part of the submission:
• Ethical AI and Dynamic Tokens – Comprehensive Regulatory Framework for Real-World
Asset Tokenization
• Enhanced Governance Framework for Regulated AI and Automated Decision-Making
Systems
• Self-Sovereign Intellectual Property Rights Framework – Digital Asset Infrastructure for IP
Tokenization and Management
• Practical Example of IoT-Enabled Tokenization
This proposal is presented as a contribution to the ongoing dialogue surrounding the evolution of
digital asset regulation and innovation. It builds upon prior recommendations I have submitted to
the Commission, and I remain deeply appreciative of the opportunity to continue this collaborative
engagement.
The SEC’s commitment to public participation through accessible and transparent platforms
exemplifies the strength of the U.S. regulatory system. By fostering inclusivity and merit-based
policy development, the Commission reinforces democratic principles while enabling responsible
technological advancement.
Prepared with diligence and a spirit of constructive contribution, this proposal recognizes the United
States’ pivotal role in shaping secure and innovative capital markets. It seeks to advance the
modernization of asset tokenization practices, ensuring investor protection, regulatory clarity, and
alignment with national priorities in economic and technological progress.
To facilitate the review and analysis of this comprehensive framework, I place myself at the full
disposal of the Commission's staff. I would be pleased to offer a personal presentation of the key
findings, participate in technical workshops, or provide any necessary clarifications, either virtually
or in person at your offices. My primary objective is to contribute constructively to the development
of a secure and innovative regulatory environment.
I commend the SEC for maintaining this open forum for meaningful participation. It empowers
contributors to help shape forward-looking financial systems rooted in integrity, excellence, and
innovation.
Respectfully submitted,

Glossary of Key Terms
IoT-Enabled Tokenization of Physical Assets with Verifiable Physical
Proof
A
Accredited Investor: An individual or entity that meets specific financial criteria under SEC Rule
501 of Regulation D, including: (1) individuals with net worth exceeding $1 million (excluding
primary residence), or (2) individuals with annual income exceeding $200,000 ($300,000 jointly
with spouse) in each of the two most recent years with reasonable expectation of same income level
in current year.
AES (Advanced Encryption Standard): Symmetric encryption algorithm approved by NIST as
FIPS 197, using 128, 192, or 256-bit key sizes for encrypting sensitive data in IoT devices and
blockchain systems.
Alternative Trading System (ATS): Non-exchange trading venue registered with the SEC under
Regulation ATS (17 CFR 242.300-303) that facilitates secondary market transactions in securities,
including tokenized assets.
AML (Anti-Money Laundering): Set of procedures, laws, and regulations designed to prevent
criminals from disguising illegally obtained funds as legitimate income, required under Bank
Secrecy Act and implemented through FinCEN regulations.
API (Application Programming Interface): Standardized set of protocols and tools enabling
software applications to communicate and exchange data, essential for oracle integration and
blockchain interoperability.
Asset-Backed Security: Security whose value and income payments derive from and are
collateralized by a specified pool of underlying assets, applicable to tokenized physical assets under
SEC regulatory framework.
Atomic Swap: Cryptographic protocol enabling exchange of one cryptocurrency or token for
another without intermediaries, using hash time-locked contracts for secure cross-chain
transactions.
B
Bank Secrecy Act (BSA): Federal law requiring financial institutions to assist government agencies
in detecting and preventing money laundering (31 U.S.C. § 5311 et seq.), applicable to tokenization
platforms as money services businesses.
Beneficial Owner: Person or entity that enjoys benefits of ownership of security or asset, even
when title is held in another name, subject to Section 13(d) reporting requirements when ownership
exceeds 5% threshold.
13

Blockchain: Distributed ledger technology using cryptographically linked blocks to record
transactions across multiple computers, providing transparent and immutable record of asset
ownership and transfers.
Blue Sky Laws: State-level securities regulations requiring registration of securities offerings and
broker-dealers, applicable to tokenized asset offerings unless preempted by federal registration or
Tier 2 Regulation A+ offerings.
Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT): Property of distributed systems enabling continued operation
despite malicious or failing components, essential for oracle consensus mechanisms with up to 33%
fault tolerance.
C
CBDC (Central Bank Digital Currency): Digital form of sovereign currency issued and regulated
by central bank, with integration considerations for future tokenization platforms.
CCPA/CPRA (California Consumer Privacy Act/California Privacy Rights Act): California
state privacy law granting consumers rights regarding personal data collection, use, and deletion,
applicable to tokenization platforms operating in California.
Chainlink: Decentralized oracle network providing external data to smart contracts through
cryptographically secured data feeds, serving as industry reference for oracle architecture.
CLARITY Act (Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act): Federal legislation establishing framework
for digital commodity classification and jurisdictional boundaries between SEC and CFTC
oversight.
Common Criteria (ISO/IEC 15408): International standard for computer security certification
providing framework for evaluating security properties of IT products through Evaluation
Assurance Levels (EAL 1-7).
Consensus Mechanism: Protocol by which distributed network participants agree on single data
value or state of network, essential for oracle networks and blockchain validation.
Crypto Task Force: SEC initiative led by Commissioner Hester M. Peirce to develop regulatory
frameworks for digital assets, focusing on security classification, jurisdictional clarity, and
registration pathways.
Custodian: Entity legally responsible for safeguarding financial assets, must be qualified under
Investment Advisers Act Rule 206(4)-2, including banks, broker-dealers, and approved digital asset
custodians.
D
DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization): Organization represented by rules encoded as
computer program on blockchain, controlled by organization members rather than central authority,
with governance implications for tokenized assets.
DApp (Decentralized Application): Application running on peer-to-peer network rather than
single computer, typically built on blockchain platforms like Ethereum.
14

DCM (Designated Contract Market): CFTC-registered exchange for trading futures contracts and
derivatives, relevant for tokenized commodity derivatives under Commodity Exchange Act.
DeFi (Decentralized Finance): Financial applications built on blockchain technology eliminating
intermediaries, including automated market makers and lending protocols for tokenized assets.
DID (Decentralized Identifier): W3C standard for self-sovereign digital identity enabling
verifiable, decentralized identification for compliance with KYC requirements.
Digital Commodity: Classification under CLARITY Act for tokens operating on sufficiently
decentralized blockchains without central entity control, subject to CFTC jurisdiction rather than
SEC.
Digital Twin: Virtual representation of physical asset containing real-time data from IoT sensors,
enabling remote monitoring and verification of tokenized asset condition.
DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act): EU regulation establishing ICT risk management
framework for financial entities, applicable to European operations of tokenization platforms.
E
EAL (Evaluation Assurance Level): Rating system in Common Criteria (ISO/IEC 15408)
indicating depth of security evaluation, ranging from EAL1 (basic) to EAL7 (highest assurance).
Edge Computing: Distributed computing paradigm processing data near source of generation (IoT
devices) rather than centralized cloud, reducing latency for real-time asset verification.
ERC-20: Ethereum token standard for fungible tokens, defining common interface for token
creation and transfer on Ethereum blockchain.
ERC-721: Ethereum token standard for non-fungible tokens (NFTs), enabling unique digital
representation of individual physical assets.
ERC-1155: Multi-token standard supporting both fungible and non-fungible tokens in single smart
contract, efficient for diverse asset portfolios.
Escrow: Legal arrangement where third party holds assets on behalf of two other parties completing
transaction, commonly used in tokenized asset transfers for regulatory compliance.
F
FATF (Financial Action Task Force): International organization developing standards for
combating money laundering and terrorist financing, issuing guidance on virtual asset service
providers.
FedRAMP (Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program): U.S. government program
providing standardized security assessment for cloud service providers, requiring FIPS 140-2
compliance.
Fiduciary Duty: Legal obligation to act in best interest of another party, applicable to asset
managers, custodians, and tokenization platform operators under Investment Advisers Act.
15

FinCEN (Financial Crimes Enforcement Network): Bureau of U.S. Department of Treasury
responsible for combating money laundering and terrorist financing, regulating virtual currency
exchanges as money services businesses.
FIPS 140-2/140-3 (Federal Information Processing Standard): U.S. government standard for
cryptographic module security with four levels, required for protecting sensitive government
information and recommended for financial applications.
FN-DSA (FFT over NTRU-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm): Post-quantum digital
signature algorithm based on FALCON, providing compact signatures for bandwidth-constrained
applications.
G
Gas Fee: Transaction fee on Ethereum blockchain paid to miners/validators for processing
transactions and executing smart contracts, consideration for tokenization platform economics.
GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation): EU regulation on data protection and privacy,
requiring specific considerations for blockchain immutability and right to erasure.
GENIUS Act (Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins): Federal
legislation establishing framework for dollar-backed stablecoins with 100% reserve requirement,
signed July 18, 2025.
Geofencing: Virtual boundary using GPS or RFID technology to trigger responses when device
enters or exits area, used for IoT device location verification and transfer restrictions.
H
Hash Function: Mathematical algorithm converting input data into fixed-size string of characters,
providing data integrity verification and forming basis of blockchain technology.
HQC (Hamming Quasi-Cyclic): Code-based post-quantum encryption algorithm selected by NIST
as backup to ML-KEM, providing mathematical diversity against quantum attacks.
HSM (Hardware Security Module): Physical computing device safeguarding and managing
digital keys for strong authentication and crypto-processing, required at FIPS 140-2 Level 3 or
higher for financial applications.
Howey Test: Supreme Court test from SEC v. W.J. Howey Co. determining whether transaction
qualifies as investment contract (security), examining: (1) investment of money, (2) common
enterprise, (3) expectation of profits, (4) from efforts of others.
Hybrid Cryptography: Combination of traditional and post-quantum cryptographic algorithms
during transition period (2025-2027), providing security against both classical and quantum attacks.
I
Immutable: Property of blockchain data that cannot be altered or deleted after recording, providing
permanent audit trail but requiring special consideration for privacy regulations.
16

Initial Coin Offering (ICO): Fundraising mechanism where new cryptocurrency tokens are sold to
investors, typically subject to securities regulation unless properly structured as utility token.
Investment Contract: Type of security under Howey test involving investment in common
enterprise with expectation of profits from others' efforts, primary classification framework for
tokenized assets.
IoT (Internet of Things): Network of physical devices embedded with sensors, software, and
connectivity enabling data collection and exchange for remote monitoring of tokenized assets.
IP Rating (Ingress Protection): IEC 60529 standard classifying degree of protection against
intrusion of solid objects and liquids, minimum IP65 required for outdoor IoT device deployment.
K
KEM (Key Encapsulation Mechanism): Cryptographic algorithm enabling two parties to
establish shared secret key over public channel, fundamental to post-quantum encryption (ML-
KEM).
KYC (Know Your Customer): Process of verifying identity of clients to prevent fraud, money
laundering, and terrorist financing, required under Bank Secrecy Act and implemented through CIP
requirements.
L
Layer 2: Secondary framework or protocol built on top of existing blockchain to improve
scalability and transaction speed, essential for high-volume IoT data processing.
Liquidity Pool: Smart contract holding reserves of multiple tokens enabling decentralized trading
through automated market maker algorithms, applicable to tokenized asset secondary markets.
LoRaWAN (Long Range Wide Area Network): Low-power wireless protocol for IoT devices
enabling long-range communication, used as backup connectivity for remote asset monitoring.
M
Market Maker: Entity providing liquidity by simultaneously posting buy and sell quotes, essential
for tokenized asset secondary market development under ATS framework.
MiCA (Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation): EU comprehensive regulatory framework for
crypto-assets establishing licensing, disclosure, and operational requirements for service providers.
ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm): NIST-standardized post-
quantum signature algorithm (FIPS 204) based on CRYSTALS-Dilithium, primary standard for
digital authentication.
ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism): NIST-standardized post-
quantum encryption algorithm (FIPS 203) based on CRYSTALS-Kyber, primary standard for
general encryption.
MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport): Lightweight messaging protocol for IoT
devices with quality of service levels, used for sensor data transmission to oracle networks.
17

Multi-Signature (Multisig): Cryptographic scheme requiring multiple parties to approve
transaction before execution, used for governance and security in smart contract upgrades.
N
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology): U.S. agency developing technology
standards including cybersecurity frameworks, cryptographic algorithms, and IoT security
guidelines.
Non-Fungible Token (NFT): Unique digital token representing specific asset on blockchain, used
for tokenizing individual physical assets with distinct characteristics.
NVLAP (National Voluntary Laboratory Accreditation Program): NIST program accrediting
testing laboratories for cryptographic module validation under FIPS 140-2/140-3.
O
OFAC (Office of Foreign Assets Control): Treasury department office administering economic
sanctions programs, requiring real-time screening of tokenized asset transactions against SDN list.
Oracle: System providing external real-world data to blockchain smart contracts, critical for
verifying physical asset existence and condition through IoT device integration.
OTC (Over-the-Counter): Trading occurring directly between parties outside formal exchanges,
relevant for private tokenized asset transfers under Regulation D exemptions.
P
PCAOB (Public Company Accounting Oversight Board): Nonprofit corporation overseeing
audits of public companies, establishing auditing standards applicable to tokenized asset financial
statements.
Physical Unclonable Function (PUF): Physical security primitive deriving unique identifier from
manufacturing variations, used for IoT device authentication preventing cloning.
Post-Quantum Cryptography: Cryptographic algorithms resistant to attacks by quantum
computers, including ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, and HQC standardized by NIST.
Private Placement: Securities offering exempt from registration under Section 4(a)(2) or
Regulation D, common structure for initial tokenized asset distributions.
Project Crypto: SEC initiative announced July 31, 2025, by Chairman Paul Atkins to modernize
securities rules for on-chain financial markets, including tokenization frameworks.
Proof of Stake (PoS): Blockchain consensus mechanism where validators are chosen based on
token holdings, energy-efficient alternative to Proof of Work for tokenization platforms.
Protection Profile (PP): ISO/IEC 15408 document specifying security requirements for class of
security devices, used as template for IoT device security evaluation.
18

Q
Qualified Custodian: Entity meeting SEC requirements under Investment Advisers Act Rule
206(4)-2, including banks, broker-dealers, and FCMs approved for digital asset custody.
Qualified Purchaser: Investor meeting high net worth thresholds under Investment Company Act
Section 2(a)(51), enabling investment in Section 3(c)(7) exempt funds.
Quantum Computing: Computing technology using quantum mechanical phenomena to solve
complex problems, posing future threat to current cryptographic systems requiring post-quantum
migration.
R
REA (Real Estate Asset): Physical property suitable for tokenization including commercial,
residential, and infrastructure assets with IoT monitoring capabilities.
Regulation ATS: SEC rule 17 CFR 242.300-303 governing alternative trading systems,
establishing registration, disclosure, and operational requirements for tokenized asset platforms.
Regulation D: SEC rules 501-508 providing exemptions from registration for private placement
offerings, most common framework for initial token distributions.
RegTech (Regulatory Technology): Technology solutions automating compliance monitoring,
reporting, and risk management for tokenization platforms.
REIT (Real Estate Investment Trust): Company owning income-producing real estate, structural
consideration for real estate tokenization under Investment Company Act.
Restricted Security: Security acquired in unregistered private sale with resale restrictions under
Rule 144, typical classification for privately placed tokenized assets.
S
SAR (Suspicious Activity Report): FinCEN form required when financial institution detects
suspicious transactions potentially involving money laundering, fraud, or terrorist financing.
SDN (Specially Designated National): OFAC list of individuals and entities with whom U.S.
persons are prohibited from conducting business, requiring real-time screening for token transfers.
Security Target (ST): ISO/IEC 15408 document specifying security requirements for specific
product, detailing how product implements protection profile requirements.
Security Token: Digital asset representing ownership interest in real-world asset that qualifies as
security under federal securities laws, subject to SEC regulation.

Executive Summary
This comprehensive framework proposes an innovative approach to tokenizing physical, real-world
assets through Internet of Things (IoT) devices that provide reliable, verifiable physical verification.
The framework builds upon recent developments in the digital asset space that aim to establish a
clear regulatory framework for digital assets, while encouraging innovation and enabling a pathway
of compliance for eligible current market participants. The system ensures that each token
corresponds to a physical asset whose condition, existence, and attributes are regularly and securely
monitored through advanced cryptographic protocols and regulatory compliance mechanisms.
The framework addresses critical market needs identified by the Securities and Exchange
Commission (SEC), aligning with President Trump's executive order entitled "Strengthening
American Leadership in Digital Financial Technology" and the establishment by the Securities and
Exchange Commission (SEC) of a Crypto Task Force. This comprehensive approach enhances trust,
reduces fraud, enables fractional ownership, and maintains strict compliance with U.S. securities
law while leveraging cutting-edge IoT technology and quantum-resistant cryptographic protocols.
The real estate tokenization market alone is projected to surge from $3.5 billion in 2024 to $19.4
billion by 2033, with a remarkable 21% yearly growth, while the asset tokenization market is
projected to reach a valuation of $2.08 trillion in 2025, with expectations to grow at a CAGR of
45.46%, hitting $13.55 trillion by 2030. This unprecedented growth trajectory demonstrates the
critical need for comprehensive regulatory frameworks that can accommodate technological
innovation while maintaining investor protection.
1. Introduction and Regulatory Context
1.1 Market Context and Regulatory Evolution
The tokenization market has experienced explosive growth, with recent developments in the digital
asset space aiming to establish a clear regulatory framework for digital assets, while encouraging
innovation and enabling a pathway of compliance for eligible current market participants. The
Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has issued statements supporting the commercialization of
asset tokenization, and financial institutions like UBS have launched services such as UBS
Tokenize, described as "a full-service offer for digital asset services" that "supports opportunities
across origination, distribution, and custody, initially focusing on tokenization of bonds, funds, and
structured products".

The real-world asset (RWA) tokenization market has grown by 380% in just three years, reaching
$24 billion this month in a sign that traditional finance is finding benefits from embracing
blockchain technology. Projections for market growth vary significantly, with McKinsey predicting
it to become a $2 trillion market, while BCG estimates $16 trillion by 2030, and Standard Chartered
projecting growth to $30 trillion by 2034.
1.2 Current SEC Framework and Leadership Evolution
The SEC's 2025 cryptocurrency guidelines mark a pivotal moment, offering much-needed clarity on
which tokens are classified as securities through an updated application of the Howey test and a
clearer system to differentiate between security tokens and non-security tokens. In a July 9, 2025,
statement ("Enchanting, but Not Magical: A Statement on the Tokenization of Securities"),
Commissioner Hester M. Peirce said that tokenized, blockchain-based versions of stocks, bonds, or
other securities remain subject to existing federal securities laws.
The new US administration promises a new approach to regulating digital and crypto assets, with
the SEC's new Crypto Task Force and the Executive Order on digital assets refocusing US policy,
calling for a clear US regulatory and legislative framework on digital assets. Commissioner Hester
Peirce, leader of the SEC's newly established Crypto Task Force, published a statement outlining
the Task Force's 10 main areas of focus, including the security status of digital assets, defining the
SEC's jurisdiction, relief for token offerings, registration issues, and a path forward for broker-
dealers and custodying digital assets.
The guidance introduces a three-pronged framework for token classification: initial sale context
(whether the token was marketed as an investment), ongoing use (if the token provides functional
utility on a decentralized network), and issuer influence (degree of control retained by the founding
team or foundation).
1.3 Legislative Framework Development
The Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act sets up a
long-awaited, uniform federal framework for dollar-backed stablecoins. The bill passed with broad
bipartisan support (68–30 in the Senate and 308–122 in the House), and was signed into law by
President Trump on July 18, 2025. The law requires that all stablecoin issuers maintain high-quality
liquid assets (such as cash or short-term U.S. Treasuries) equal to 100% of the value of tokens in
circulation.
The Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act, passed by the House with a 294–134 vote, confronts one
of crypto's most debated legal questions: when should a token be treated as a security, and when is it
a commodity? The bill introduces the term digital commodity, referring to tokens operating on
sufficiently decentralized or mature blockchains where no single entity exerts control.
1.4 Federal Digital Asset Policy Coordination

(the "Working Group") within the National Economic Council, chaired by David Sacks, the White
House's Special Advisor for AI and Crypto, with membership including federal agency leaders

including the secretary of the treasury, chairman of the SEC, and chairman of the CFTC. This high-

7. Securities Law Classification and Regulatory Compliance
7.1 Howey Test Application to IoT-Enabled Tokens
The SEC applies the Howey Test as the primary legal framework to determine whether a digital
asset is a security, examining whether a transaction involves: (1) an investment of money, (2) in a
common enterprise, (3) with a reasonable expectation of profits, (4) derived from the efforts of
others. IoT-enabled tokenization presents unique considerations for each prong of this analysis.
7.1.1 Investment of Money Analysis
The first prong of the Howey Test is typically satisfied in tokenization scenarios:
Traditional Investment Structures:
• Direct purchase of tokens with fiat currency or cryptocurrency

• Contribution of existing assets in exchange for tokenized ownership interests
• Investment of services or other consideration in exchange for tokens
• Subscription agreements with installment payment structures
Enhanced Due Diligence for IoT Assets:
• Valuation requirements for physical assets with independent appraisal verification
• Technical due diligence on IoT infrastructure and monitoring capabilities
• Legal due diligence on property title, liens, and encumbrances
• Insurance verification and adequacy analysis for asset protection
7.1.2 Common Enterprise Analysis
The common enterprise prong requires careful analysis in tokenized asset structures:
Horizontal Common Enterprise:
• Pooling of investor funds to acquire or manage physical assets
• Shared profits and losses among all token holders
• Proportional rights to asset income and appreciation
• Collective decision-making on material asset management decisions
Vertical Common Enterprise:
• Token holder fortunes tied to the efforts and success of asset managers
• Dependence on promoter expertise for asset selection and management
• Reliance on third-party service providers for asset maintenance and operation
• Success tied to overall performance of tokenization platform or ecosystem
7.1.3 Expectation of Profits Analysis
This prong is often the most complex in tokenization scenarios, requiring analysis of investor
motivations and token economics:
Traditional Profit Sources:
• Rental income from real estate assets distributed to token holders
• Appreciation in underlying asset value reflected in token price
• Revenue sharing from income-producing assets (equipment leasing, etc.)
• Capital gains from eventual asset sale or liquidation
IoT-Specific Value Propositions:
• Data monetization from IoT sensors creating additional revenue streams
• Efficiency improvements from smart asset management reducing costs
• Enhanced transparency providing premium valuations for verified assets
• Reduced operational costs through automated monitoring and maintenance
7.1.4 Efforts of Others Analysis
The final Howey prong examines whether investor returns depend primarily on the efforts of third
parties:

Advanced Technical Implementation of Explainable AI Systems
The framework mandates implementation of multiple explainability techniques that provide
complementary perspectives on AI decision-making processes. SHAP (SHapley Additive

slight changes in input variables might affect outcomes. These explanations must be generated in
real-time for customer-facing applications and stored for regulatory review in all cases.
Counterfactual explanation systems must be implemented to demonstrate how decisions would
change under alternative scenarios, particularly focusing on scenarios that address potential bias
concerns. These systems must be designed to identify the minimal changes required to achieve
different outcomes, helping customers understand actionable steps for improving their financial
situations.
The framework requires implementation of attention mechanism visualization for neural network-
based systems, providing insight into which input features or data elements most strongly influence
specific decisions. These visualizations must be automatically generated for regulatory examination
and available to qualified customer representatives upon request.
Causal inference capabilities must be implemented for systems affecting material customer
outcomes, enabling analysis of whether AI systems are learning spurious correlations that could
lead to biased or unfair decisions. These systems must implement interventional analysis
capabilities that can estimate the causal impact of specific variables on outcomes.

comprehensive federal regulation of IP-related securities.
The theoretical framework recognizes intellectual property as a unique category of intangible asset
that combines aspects of both private property rights and public policy objectives. Unlike tangible
assets, IP rights exist as legal constructs created by statute, with their value dependent upon
enforceability within established legal systems. This characteristic makes IP particularly suitable for
blockchain-based management systems, as the immutable record-keeping and automated
enforcement capabilities of distributed ledger technology align with the need for clear ownership

issues highlighted in the rapidly growing RWA market, which reached $27.6 billion by mid-2025,

• Asset Description: The "Texas SunPower Solar Farm" is a 100-megawatt utility-scale solar
installation valued at $150 million, spanning 1,000 acres in West Texas. It generates
approximately 250 gigawatt-hours annually, powering 20,000 homes and contributing to
Texas's renewable energy targets. The farm features advanced photovoltaic panels and
inverters, with current challenges including financing gaps for expansion and variability in

• Regulatory Compliance Alignment:
• Classified as a security token under SEC 2025 guidelines via the updated Howey
test, representing fractional ownership in energy generation assets (Section 2.1.2).
The Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act supports treatment as a "digital commodity"
on decentralized blockchains post-issuance, while the GENIUS Act backs stablecoin
distributions for energy revenue payouts with 100% reserves in U.S. Treasuries.
• Aligned with the President's Working Group on Digital Asset Markets, emphasizing
risk management (e.g., weather-related output variability) and consumer protection
through verifiable IoT data.
• IoT Infrastructure Implementation:
• Device Deployment: Compliant with NIST standards (Section 3.1), the farm is
outfitted with IoT sensors including:
• Environmental monitors for temperature, humidity, and solar irradiance to
track condition attributes (Section 2.2.2).
• Performance sensors on panels and inverters measuring output efficiency,
uptime, and fault detection for operational metrics.
• GPS and security systems for location verification and perimeter protection
against tampering or theft (Section 2.2.1).
• Security Standards: Devices use ML-KEM-768 for quantum-resistant key exchange

on critical alerts, Section 3.2.2), and zero-trust networking over redundant channels
(5G primary, satellite tertiary, Section 3.2.3).
• Monitoring for Revenue and Usage: Integration with utility meters and grid
systems tracks real-time energy generation and revenue (Section 2.2.3), with AI-
driven analytics predicting maintenance needs.
• Tokenization Process:
• Asset Selection and Classification: Qualifies as an energy generation asset under
Section 2.1.2, with mandatory monitoring of performance (efficiency KPIs),
condition (panel integrity via vibration sensors), and usage (output metrics tied to
revenue).

• Device Installation and Commissioning: Per Section 3.3.2, devices are deployed

• Smart Contract Integration: Tokens issued on a blockchain with quantum-resistant

• Benefits and Outcomes:

Investment advisers should not be permitted to self-custody client crypto assets without full compliance with the Investment Advisers Act and related custody rules, as this would expose investors to heightened risks and conflicts of interest.
