Appendix F — Integration Realities and Technical
Debt
The cryptographic primitives underlying evidentiary compliance are well-established. The
challenge lies not in the mathematics but in grafting these proofs onto the messy reality of
enterprise systems. The following sections outline key implementation challenges - not as
insurmountable barriers, but as the predictable friction that accompanies any significant
infrastructure shift.
Key Management at Scale
Cryptographic signatures require key management, and key management at enterprise scale
is complex - though hardly unprecedented.
A mid-sized financial institution might generate 10 million receipts daily. Each needs a
signature, which raises immediate questions: What entity signs? The system? The
department? The individual processor? This isn't merely technical - it's about establishing
chains of authority that courts will recognize.
Organizations will likely adopt hierarchical signing schemes similar to their existing certificate
infrastructures. System-level keys handle bulk operations, department keys sign significant
state changes, and executive keys authorize critical assertions. Hardware Security Modules
(HSMs) protect these keys, though throughput limitations (typically 10,000
signatures/second) require distributed architectures.
Key rotation adds complexity. Financial regulations often mandate annual rotation, yet
receipts must remain verifiable for decades. This means maintaining secure archives of
historical keys - much like organizations already maintain archived encryption keys for
regulatory discovery. When banks merge, they inherit these key archives just as they inherit
legacy systems, maintaining them grudgingly but functionally.
The nightmare scenario - key compromise - has established playbooks. If a signing key is
exposed, receipts signed with that key enter a "presumed valid but under review" status,
similar to how payment card networks handle merchant breaches. Not ideal, but workable.
The State Transition Mapping Problem
Real business processes resist clean state modeling. A commercial loan application might
have 12 statuses in the origination system, 8 in credit assessment, and 23 in the servicing
platform. These don't map neatly to the "created modified validated destroyed"→ → →
lifecycle that CSTP assumes.
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 30

Organizations will solve this through selective receipting. Rather than capture every internal
state change, they'll receipt the transitions that matter for compliance: application received,
credit decision made, funds disbursed, loan closed. The internal complexity remains in
traditional logs while critical transitions get cryptographic proof.
Error states and edge cases require special handling. When a system crashes mid-transition,
organizations will likely generate "exception receipts" that document the anomaly without
breaking the chain. Think of these as cryptographic incident reports - they acknowledge
something went wrong while maintaining evidentiary continuity.
The gap between business events and system states (verbal agreements, offline decisions)
will be bridged through "attestation receipts" - human-initiated receipts that capture
significant events outside system workflows. Not perfect, but better than the current practice
of hoping someone wrote it down.
Organizational Adaptation Patterns
Every department initially resists receipt infrastructure, but resistance erodes under regulatory
pressure.
Legal teams worry about discovery implications - every receipt potentially becomes evidence.
But they worried the same about email retention, and adapted. They'll develop receipt
retention policies that balance compliance requirements with litigation risk, likely keeping
receipts for required periods then destroying them under documented legal holds.
Operations teams concerned about latency will find that 30 microseconds of receipt
generation is negligible compared to network variance. High-frequency trading systems
already handle similar overhead from regulatory reporting requirements. Customer-facing
systems will buffer receipt generation asynchronously, maintaining responsiveness while
ensuring compliance.
Compliance teams lose some narrative flexibility - receipts provide binary proof rather than
explanatory wiggle room. But they gain something more valuable: defensible positions. "We
have cryptographic proof" ends many regulatory inquiries that would otherwise consume
weeks of explanation.
IT departments facing integration costs will proceed incrementally. They'll start with new
systems (easier to build in than bolt on), then tackle critical legacy systems during planned
modernization. Less critical systems might never get receipt capability - they'll remain in the
procedural compliance world until retirement.
How This Actually Unfolds
The adoption pattern is predictable because we've seen it before with SOX, GDPR, and Basel
III. Here's the likely progression:
©2025, Epistria, LLC All Rights Reserved 31

Year 1-2: Pioneer Phase A few forward-thinking organizations implement receipts for narrow,
high-risk use cases. Perhaps a bank implements destruction receipts for GDPR compliance,
or a healthcare system adds lifecycle receipts for clinical trials. These implementations are
expensive, custom, and imperfect. But they work well enough to prevent a major fine or win a
lawsuit.
Year 3-4: Standardization Industry bodies develop receipt standards - likely competing ones
initially. Cloud providers offer "receipt as a service" APIs. Enterprise software vendors add
receipt generation to their platforms (badly at first, but improving under customer pressure).
The first major enforcement action where receipts would have prevented disaster makes
headlines.
Year 5-7: Adoption Cascade Regulators begin "strongly encouraging" receipt use without
mandating it. Cyber insurance companies offer premium discounts for organizations with
receipt coverage. System integrators develop migration playbooks. The technology becomes
boring - a checkbox feature rather than competitive advantage.
Year 8-10: New Normal Fresh graduates learn receipt-based compliance in school. Legacy
systems without receipts require special exemptions. Regulators mandate receipts for critical
sectors. Organizations compete on receipt coverage percentages in their annual reports.
Throughout this progression, implementations remain imperfect. Coverage is partial - perhaps
60% of critical transitions in Year 5, growing to 85% by Year 10. Some receipts are lost to
system failures. Key management occasionally fails. Courts struggle with technical details.
But even imperfect cryptographic evidence beats perfect procedural attestation. An
organization with receipts for most critical transitions faces regulatory scrutiny with
confidence. One without them hopes their narrative holds up.
The transition won't be smooth, cheap, or complete. But it's as inevitable as double-entry
bookkeeping was for Renaissance merchants or SOX compliance was for public companies.
The organizations that move early will shape the standards, influence the regulations, and
avoid the panic implementations that follow the first major enforcement actions.
Evidentiary debt is real. The tools to address it exist. The only question is whether
organizations act before or after the next collapse makes headlines.

Glossary of Key Terms
1. Circuit Breaker A pre-programmed, automated mechanism designed to temporarily halt trading
or other smart contract functions in response to extreme market volatility or detected security
anomalies. The framework proposes a hybrid model combining automated triggers with human
oversight.
2. DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization) An organization represented by rules encoded
as a computer program (smart contracts) that is controlled by its members and not influenced by a
central authority. The framework proposes methods for attributing legal responsibility to DAO
participants.
3. DeFi (Decentralized Finance) An ecosystem of blockchain-based financial applications that
operate without central financial intermediaries, such as brokerages, exchanges, or banks.
4. "Effects Test" A legal principle used to assert U.S. jurisdiction over conduct occurring outside
the United States if it has a substantial effect on U.S. investors or markets.
5. Formal Verification A rigorous method of proving or disproving the correctness of a smart
contract's underlying algorithms with respect to a certain formal specification or property, using
mathematical proofs. This goes beyond standard testing and auditing.
6. HSM (Hardware Security Module) A physical computing device that safeguards and manages
digital keys for strong authentication and provides crypto-processing. The framework mandates
HSMs certified at FIPS 140-2 Level 3 or higher for all critical cryptographic operations.
7. Homomorphic Encryption A form of encryption that allows computation to be performed on
encrypted data without decrypting it first. It is a key technology proposed in the framework to
enable privacy-preserving regulatory analysis.
8. IOSCO (International Organization of Securities Commissions) An international body that
brings together the world's securities regulators and is recognized as the global standard-setter for
the securities sector. The proposal aligns with IOSCO's policy recommendations for digital assets.
9. MPC (Multi-Party Computation) A cryptographic technology that allows multiple parties to
jointly compute a function over their inputs while keeping those inputs private. In the context of this
framework, it is primarily used for secure management of private keys in custody solutions.
10. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) A U.S. federal agency that develops
technology, metrics, and standards. The framework mandates compliance with NIST's
Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 and its standards for blockchain technology and post-quantum
cryptography.
11. On-Chain Refers to transactions, data, or interactions that are recorded and verified directly on
a blockchain or other distributed ledger.
9

12. PQC (Quantum-Resistant Cryptography) Cryptographic algorithms that are thought to be
secure against attacks by quantum computers. The framework mandates PQC to ensure the long-
term security of tokenized sovereign debt instruments.
13. Regulatory Oracle A trusted and independent data feed designed specifically to provide
verifiable, real-time information to smart contracts and regulators for the purpose of supervision and
compliance. Key functions include verifying asset backing, market data, and reputational metrics.
14. Regulatory Sandbox A controlled environment established by the SEC that allows firms to test
innovative financial products, services, or business models with real customers, subject to specific
safeguards and oversight, without immediately incurring all the normal regulatory consequences.
15. Slashing An economic penalty mechanism in proof-of-stake or oracle networks where a
validator or data provider that misbehaves (e.g., provides false data or goes offline) has a portion of
their staked tokens seized and destroyed.
16. Smart Contract A self-executing program that runs on a blockchain, with the terms of an
agreement between parties being directly written into lines of code.
17. Tokenized Sovereign Debt A digital token that represents a legal claim on a debt instrument
issued by a national government (e.g., a U.S. Treasury Bill). These tokens are recorded, issued, and
transferred on a blockchain.
18. ZKP (Zero-Knowledge Proof) A cryptographic method by which one party (the prover) can
prove to another party (the verifier) that they know a value, without conveying any information
apart from the fact that they know the value. It is proposed to enable compliance verification while
preserving privacy.

FOR GOVERNANCE OF TOKENIZED

Submission to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
This document presents a comprehensive proposal directed to the U.S. Securities and Exchange
Commission (SEC) for the establishment of an ethical, modular, and auditable regulatory
framework specifically designed to supervise tokenized assets linked to United States sovereign
debt. This proposal does not interfere with the primary issuance of public securities, which remains
the exclusive prerogative of the U.S. Treasury and the Federal Reserve. Instead, it focuses on
regulating secondary markets and protecting investors in the emerging tokenized sovereign debt
ecosystem.
The framework addresses critical regulatory gaps in the digital asset space while maintaining
alignment with existing securities law precedents and regulatory authorities' jurisdictional
boundaries. This proposal enhances transparency, reduces regulatory capture risks, and creates a
more secure and reliable secondary market environment for tokenized sovereign debt instruments.
Technical Foundation and Regulatory Alignment
This framework is designed to align with the SEC's "Project Crypto" initiative announced by
Chairman Paul Atkins in July 2025, which aims to modernize securities regulations for blockchain-
based assets. The framework incorporates the principles outlined in the SEC's comprehensive
initiative to enable America's financial markets to move "on-chain" while maintaining investor
protection and market integrity standards.
The proposal builds upon the fundamental principle that tokenized securities remain securities
regardless of their technological implementation, ensuring that all tokenized sovereign debt
instruments maintain compliance with federal securities laws while leveraging the efficiency
benefits of distributed ledger technology.
Integration with International Standards
The framework incorporates the latest international regulatory standards, including IOSCO's 18
policy recommendations for crypto and digital asset markets, which establish clear international
regulatory baselines for crypto asset service providers. The framework specifically addresses the
BIS Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (CPMI) and IOSCO joint guidance on
stablecoin arrangements and systemically important payment infrastructures, ensuring compatibility
with global regulatory trends.
The technical architecture leverages NIST blockchain technology standards and cybersecurity
frameworks, including the enhanced distributed ledger technology protocols and tamper-resistant
11

digital ledger implementations to ensure robust security and auditability throughout the tokenization
ecosystem.
1. INTRODUCTION
1.1 Regulatory Context and Scope
The emergence of tokenized assets representing claims on sovereign debt instruments presents
novel challenges for securities regulation. While the SEC lacks authority over primary sovereign
debt issuance, its jurisdiction extends to:
• Trading platforms for tokenized assets
• Tokens that constitute securities under federal law
• Public offerings including Initial Coin Offerings (ICOs), Security Token Offerings (STOs),
and token offerings
• Conduct of licensed issuers and broker-dealers
• Systemic risk management in regulated markets
This framework proposal operates within these established jurisdictional boundaries while
addressing the unique characteristics of tokenized sovereign debt instruments.
1.2 Legal Foundation and Compliance Framework
The proposed framework builds upon existing securities law infrastructure, including:
• Securities Act of 1933 registration and disclosure requirements
• Securities Exchange Act of 1934 market integrity provisions
• Investment Company Act of 1940 and Investment Advisers Act protections
• Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) anti-money laundering requirements
• Commodity Exchange Act provisions for derivative instruments
1.3 Technical Infrastructure and Standards Compliance
1.3.1 NIST Cybersecurity Framework Integration
The framework mandates compliance with NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 standards across
five core functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover. All tokenized asset providers
must implement comprehensive cybersecurity programs addressing:
Identification Requirements: Complete asset inventory including smart contracts, oracle
networks, custody systems, and data repositories with real-time monitoring capabilities and
automated discovery protocols.
Protection Standards: Implementation of advanced cryptographic protocols, multi-signature
custody solutions, and zero-knowledge proof systems for privacy-preserving compliance
verification while maintaining regulatory transparency.
12

Detection Capabilities: Deployment of AI-powered anomaly detection systems capable of
identifying market manipulation, unusual trading patterns, and potential security vulnerabilities in
real-time across distributed ledger networks.
Response Protocols: Automated incident response procedures with predetermined escalation paths,
smart contract circuit breakers, and coordinated regulatory notification systems meeting sub-minute
response requirements for critical incidents.
Recovery Mechanisms: Comprehensive business continuity planning including cross-chain asset
recovery procedures, backup oracle networks, and investor protection protocols ensuring minimal
disruption during system failures or security incidents.
1.3.2 Blockchain Technical Standards and Interoperability
The framework establishes technical requirements based on NIST blockchain technology guidelines
and distributed ledger standards, ensuring tamper-evident and tamper-resistant transaction recording
across multiple blockchain protocols:
Consensus Mechanism Requirements: All supported blockchain networks must implement
byzantine fault-tolerant consensus algorithms with demonstrated security against economic attacks
and maintaining finality guarantees suitable for financial instrument settlement.
Interoperability Standards: Cross-chain compatibility requirements enabling seamless asset
portability between compliant blockchain networks while maintaining audit trails and regulatory
oversight capabilities across all supported protocols.
Smart Contract Security: Implementation of formal verification requirements for all smart
contracts handling tokenized sovereign debt, including automated security scanning, economic
model validation, and governance mechanism analysis.
Data Oracle Architecture: Integration of multiple independent data sources with cryptographic
validation, real-time performance monitoring, and automated failover capabilities to ensure accurate
and tamper-proof external data feeds.
1.3.3 Supervised Federated Gateways for Cross-Chain Interoperability
To ensure the systemic integrity and regulatory coherence of the tokenized sovereign debt market,
this framework mandates that all cross-chain interoperability and value transfer must be conducted
through Supervised Federated Gateways. A Federated Gateway is defined as a cross-chain bridge
managed and operated by a consortium of SEC-certified and supervised entities, such as qualified
custodians, registered broker-dealers, and certified oracle providers. This model is the exclusive
mechanism permitted for moving tokenized sovereign debt between different blockchain networks
under this framework, ensuring that a complete and unbroken chain of regulatory oversight is
maintained at all times.
This approach stands in stark contrast to the operational models of many existing decentralized and
anonymous bridges, which have historically proven to be significant sources of systemic risk,
frequent targets of catastrophic hacks, and conduits for illicit financial activities. By design, the
Federated Gateway model establishes clear legal and operational accountability, provides a robust
framework for implementing AML/CFT controls consistent with the FATF Travel Rule, and offers a
13

definitive point of contact for regulatory supervision and incident response. This preemptively
mitigates the risk of contagion from external protocol failures and reinforces the security perimeter
of the regulated market.

9.1.2 Enhanced Enforcement Strategy for Decentralized Protocols
To address the practical challenges of enforcing regulations against decentralized or anonymous
actors, this framework proposes a layered and pragmatic enforcement strategy that extends beyond
direct protocol intervention:
• Focus on Centralized Touchpoints: The primary enforcement vector will target regulated,
centralized intermediaries that provide the critical bridge between the decentralized protocol
and the U.S. financial system. This includes a strict liability standard for fiat on-ramps/off-
ramps, wallet providers, and front-end operators that facilitate access for U.S. persons to
non-compliant protocols.
• Inter-Agency Collaboration: A formal memorandum of understanding (MOU) will be
established between the SEC, FinCEN, the Department of Justice (DOJ), and OFAC to
create a joint task force for decentralized finance. This task force will leverage the unique
capabilities of each agency—combining the SEC's securities expertise with FinCEN's
financial intelligence, the DOJ's prosecutorial authority, and OFAC's sanctions power—to
build comprehensive cases against illicit actors.
• Code and Developer Liability Precedents: While acknowledging the complexities
surrounding code as speech, the framework's enforcement will focus on the conduct of
individuals or entities that exercise material control over, or derive significant financial
benefit from, a protocol that violates U.S. securities laws. This includes core developers,
governance token holders with significant voting power, and treasury managers who direct
protocol funds.
• Incentives for Proactive Compliance: The framework will establish a formal "Safe
Harbor" for protocols that proactively integrate compliance-enabling technologies. This
could include using certified regulatory oracles for sanctions screening, implementing
identity solutions for permissioned liquidity pools, or building in automated compliance
checks at the smart contract level. Protocols that achieve this certification would benefit
from a presumption of compliance, shifting the enforcement focus to truly illicit and non-
cooperative networks.

APPENDIX F: Interoperable Financial
Identity Infrastructure (IIF)
1. Introduction
The growing complexity of global financial markets, combined with regulatory fragmentation
across jurisdictions, requires a new model for interoperability of digital identities, financial
reputation, and regulatory credentials. This proposal establishes the foundations for creating an
Interoperable Financial Identity Infrastructure (IIF), based on open standards for verifiable
credentials (W3C Verifiable Credentials) and distributed ledger technology (DLT).
The central objective is to enable critical information for compliance, reputation, and identity of
investors and consultants to transit securely, auditably, and legally valid between platforms,
financial service providers, and regulatory jurisdictions (such as SEC, MiCA, FATF, etc.).
2. Objectives and Benefits
• Global Portability of Financial Identity: enable an investor or entity to migrate their
financial identity between different systems without losing compliance records, reputation,
or previous verifications.
• Reduction of Operational Redundancy: minimize repetition of KYC/AML, suitability,
and background verification processes by allowing previously validated credentials to be
safely reused.
• Cross-Border Compliance: enable diverse regulatory rules (e.g., SEC in the US, MiCA in
the EU) to be translated into interoperable and auditable credential schemas.
• Focus on Privacy and Data Sovereignty: the model favors data control by holders, with
selective cryptographic proofs (e.g., ZK-Proofs), avoiding unnecessary sharing of sensitive
data.
3. Infrastructure Components
3.1. Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) Layer
Utilization of decentralized identifiers (DIDs) and verifiable credentials according to W3C
specifications, issued by recognized regulatory, financial, and certification entities.
• Example: A qualified custodian can issue a "Qualified Investor" credential, digitally signed,
that can be used across multiple platforms.
3.2. Orchestration via Permissioned DLT
Records of issuance, revocation, and audit of credentials are maintained on permissioned DLTs,
with multilateral governance involving regulators, auditors, and infrastructure entities.
• The DLT does not store personal data, only hashes and essential metadata for verification
and integrity.
91

3.3. Regulatory Bridge between Jurisdictions
Each jurisdiction defines credential schemas compatible with its legislation (e.g., SEC Rule 206(4)-
2 or EU MiCA), with standardized semantic and logical mappings.
• Validation tools can recognize regulatory equivalences between a MiCA "suitability
verification" and an SEC one.
3.4. Application Layer with Standardized APIs
Investment advisors, regulated DeFi platforms, custodians, and auditors access the infrastructure via
standardized APIs, enabling:
• Compliance verification before transaction execution.
• Real-time auditing of profiles and activities based on active credentials.
• Profile migration between platforms without new data collection.
4. Governance and Compliance
4.1. Issuing Authorities
• Financial regulators (e.g., SEC, FINRA, ESMA).
• Qualified financial service providers (custodians, banks, brokerages).
• Certified independent auditors.
4.2. Multilateral Interoperability Committee (MIC)
• Responsible for defining and maintaining semantic and technical interoperability standards.
• Representatives from different jurisdictions, including FATF observers.
4.3. Compliance with Privacy Standards
• Structure compatible with GDPR, CCPA, and other data protection legislation.
• Implementation of cryptographic proofs of consent and authorized use.
5. Priority Use Cases
1. Migration between investment advisors without new KYC verification.
2. Faster onboarding on regulated platforms.
3. Cross-border transactions between investors and financial products.
4. Continuous compliance with regulatory oracles without raw data exposure.
5. Automated continuous auditing and reporting.
6. Security and Recovery
• Use of ZK-Proofs to preserve confidentiality.
• Mechanisms for revocation, updating, and suspension of credentials.
• Operational continuity plans and cyber resilience in cases of failures or attacks on the DLT.
7. Compatibility with Existing Initiatives
• W3C Verifiable Credentials: foundation for the identity structure.

• NIST Framework for Digital Identity: compatibility with US federal standards.
• MiCA (EU) and FATF Travel Rule: semantic and legal adaptation.
8. Final Considerations
The Interoperable Financial Identity Infrastructure (IIF) represents a significant advance in the
architecture of the new digital regulatory era. By combining security, portability, compliance, and
privacy in a single interoperable model, the proposal offers reduced regulatory cost, increased
market efficiency, and greater protection for the end investor.

APPENDIX G: Interoperable Financial
Identity Infrastructure (IIF) FAQs
I. Governance and Operations
1. Governance Structure: The proposal mentions a "multilateral governance" and a "Standards
Council." How exactly would this council be formed and funded? Would it be a new nonprofit
organization, a consortium of private companies, or a body supervised by regulators like the SEC
and ESMA?
The multilateral governance of IIF is proposed as an independent nonprofit organization with
indirect regulatory oversight. This entity, provisionally called the Financial Identity Standards
Council (FISC), would be composed of:
• Representatives from regulatory bodies (e.g., SEC, CFTC, FINRA, international observers
like ESMA or IOSCO).
• Institutional participants (custodians, advisors, banks, KYC verification entities).
• Technical and legal experts in digital identity, security, and regulatory compliance.
Initial funding would come from proportional contributions from founding members and
public/private subsidies. Long-term sustainability would come from moderate administrative fees
paid by credential-issuing entities and integrated platforms.
2. Certification Process: What qualifies an entity to be a recognized credential issuer? Would there
be a formal accreditation process? Who would be responsible for auditing and certifying these
issuers to ensure they follow technical and ethical standards?
Credential issuance would be restricted to entities accredited by FISC, based on the following
criteria:
• Compliance with technical standards (e.g., W3C Verifiable Credentials, DID, OWASP).
• Operational and cybersecurity auditing.
• Regulatory history and adherence to ethical conduct standards.
Accreditation would be periodic (e.g., every 12 months) and would involve technical and legal
audits by independent third parties contracted by FISC. Serious failures would result in automatic
revocation of the issuance license.
3. Conflict Resolution: If different jurisdictions have conflicting interpretations about a credential,
how would conflicts be resolved? What would be the role of the Standards Council in mediating
disputes about "regulatory equivalence"?
Conflicts between regulatory interpretations would be handled by a Regulatory Equivalence
Committee (REC), within FISC, with experts in cross-border compliance. This committee would
have authority to:
• Evaluate and publish regulatory equivalence guidelines.
• Issue binding opinions on disputes between jurisdictions.

• Reject credentials that do not meet minimum interoperability criteria.

REC opinion about the equivalence of a MiCA rule? Would the SEC be obligated to accept the
committee's decision, or would it have veto power for operations in its jurisdiction? How does the
framework handle regulatory sovereignty?
The Regulatory Equivalence Committee (REC), within FISC, has the role of issuing binding
opinions only for members voluntarily integrated into the IIF network. However, no sovereign
regulator (like the SEC) is obligated to automatically accept such opinions.
If the SEC disagrees with an opinion about equivalence with MiCA, for example:
• The SEC maintains total veto power over operations in its jurisdiction.
• The REC opinion would have automatically suspended effect in the US until the SEC

• The framework provides for an explicit regulatory sovereignty clause, where national
authority always takes precedence.
This structure allows technical and interpretive interoperability without compromising legal

5. Continuous Monitoring of Issuers: The periodic accreditation every 12 months is good control.
However, what prevents an issuing entity from suffering a security breach or changing its internal
practices in the 2nd month of its 12-month cycle? Is there a requirement for continuous security
monitoring or a whistleblowing channel that can trigger an emergency audit?
In addition to annual periodic accreditation, IIF incorporates a continuous monitoring model
with three complementary layers:
1. Log-based automatic auditing: issuer activities are monitored in real-time through
cryptographically verifiable records.
2. Technical and regulatory whistleblowing channel: participating entities or third parties
can submit alerts to FISC, with identity protection.
3. Emergency auditing: FISC can trigger an audit outside the regular cycle based on
automatic signals (e.g., revocation anomalies) or substantiated reports.
This model mitigates reputational and operational risks in the period between two formal audits.
II. Technical Implementation and Security
6. Credential Storage: The document states that DLT does not store personal data. Where, then,
would the verifiable credentials (which contain the data) be stored? Would it be in digital wallets
controlled by the user themselves (sovereign identity model), or would they remain under the
custody of the issuing entity? What are the security implications for each model?
Verifiable credentials (VCs) would be stored in digital wallets controlled by the end user (self-
sovereign identity - SSI model). Alternatively, users could opt to delegate this storage to a trusted
identity custodian provider.
95

Security implications:
• Self-sovereign model: greater control and privacy, but requires user robustness in backup
and recovery.
• Custodian model: better technical support and recovery, but requires institutional trust.
Both models must be compatible with revocation, explicit consent, and strong authentication
standards (e.g., FIDO2).
7. Real-Time Revocation: You mention "revocation, update, and suspension mechanisms for
credentials." Could you detail how an emergency revocation would work? For example, if the SEC
revokes an advisor's license, how does this information propagate through the network instantly to
prevent fraudulent transactions?
Credential revocation follows the following technical process:
1. The issuing entity publishes the hash of the revoked credential in a permissioned DLT
registry.
2. Network nodes propagate the update to all participating platforms in seconds.
3. Verification APIs automatically access the revoked credentials list, invalidating their use in
transactions.
4. Revocation can be accompanied by explanatory metadata (e.g., "revoked by SEC regulatory
decision").
This model ensures near real-time revocation with verifiable integrity and transparency.
8. Compatibility with the "Travel Rule": The proposal focuses on privacy and zero-knowledge
proofs (ZK-Proofs). How does this model reconcile with FATF's "Travel Rule," which requires
explicit transmission of originator and beneficiary information between financial institutions in a
transaction?
IIF infrastructure can offer programmable compliance with FATF's Travel Rule via two
complementary mechanisms:
• Conditional ZK-Proofs: allow validation that the originator and beneficiary were
authenticated by recognized entities, without revealing complete data, except under valid
legal request.
• Active Compliance Mode: allows institutions to opt to transmit data explicitly when
required, maintaining immutable logs for auditing.
IIF architecture is flexible enough to adjust to specific requirements of each jurisdiction, including
offering distinct compliance modes by risk context.
9. Key Loss in Self-Sovereign Model: In the SSI model, if a user loses their private keys (e.g.,
loses device without backup), do they permanently lose their verified financial identity? Is there a
"social recovery" protocol or supervised credential re-issuance that doesn't compromise the security
of the model?
The IIF SSI model provides for a secure recovery infrastructure, based on social recovery
protocols and multi-trusted-party computation (MPC). Mechanisms include:
96

• Prior designation of trusted agents (people or institutions) who, by consensus, can
authorize key regeneration.
• Supervised re-issuance recovery: issuing entities can re-issue credentials, after rigorous
multifactor verification and auditable logs.
• Optional encrypted backup in digital vaults (custodial or self-hosted), with biometric +
physical factor authentication.
This model prevents permanent loss without compromising the structural security of the system.

but in high-frequency markets, seconds are an eternity. What is the maximum guaranteed
propagation time (SLA - Service Level Agreement) for a revocation notification across the entire
network? How does the system handle the risk of a transaction being validated by a node that hasn't
yet received the revocation update due to a temporary network partition?
IIF defines a 2-second SLA (Service Level Agreement) for propagation of revocation events
across the entire main network (permissioned mainnet), with fallback mechanisms in case of
network partition:
• Timestamp pre-verification mechanism: before authorizing a transaction, the node verifies
if the credential is updated based on the timestamp of the last synchronization.
• Prioritized critical validators: validators with direct connection to regulatory issuers
receive revocations with maximum priority.
• Temporary inconsistency tolerance: high-risk transactions (e.g., values above a certain
threshold) require double verification to mitigate latency attacks.
This significantly reduces the risk of "regulatory front-running" even in low-latency environments.

• The issuing entity responds for errors or falsifications in issued credentials.

Responsibility is distributed and hierarchical based on each party's function, in line with
regulatory principles.

to an individual's identity and transaction data? Is there an "emergency access" mechanism for legal

While data remains under the holder's control, the architecture provides for an emergency

• FISC maintains a cryptographic audit key, with mutual authorization from auditor +
regulator.

• The user is notified, except for justified legal exceptions.

• Verification of the credential's validity scope (jurisdiction, type of permitted operation).

• Ensuring that the credential is appropriate for the intended transaction type (e.g., risk

• Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) with immutable access logs and automatic legal
triggers.
• Public (or permissioned) registry of all key activations, with verifiable hashes and cross-

• Zero Trust Policy: no audit operation occurs without triple validation of court order, agent

This model seeks to balance legal compliance with protection against systemic abuse or state

• The agent may be civilly liable, if negligence is proven, especially if they didn't follow
certified protocols.
• IIF also provides for mandatory professional liability insurance (errors and omissions
insurance) for certified agents, to cover losses caused to third parties.
100

• To avoid excessive penalties in cases of systemic failure, responsibility is shared with the
credential issuer and consuming platform, according to event analysis.
20. Non-Technical User Experience: How would an ordinary citizen, without cryptography
knowledge, manage their credentials, consents, and keys securely? Couldn't the inherent complexity
of a self-sovereign model create a significant barrier to mass adoption, effectively excluding less
digitalized populations or those with less technical knowledge?
IIF recognizes the accessibility challenge and proposes a "technical complexity abstraction"
model, with the following elements:
• Intuitive graphical interfaces, with key management through biometrics, mnemonic
phrases, and digital vaults with automatic backup (opt-in).
• Certified support agents (e.g., financial institutions, public libraries, post offices) who
assist non-technical users with security and guidance.
• Hybrid operation mode: users can delegate part of the custody or management of their
credentials to regulated entities with reversible contract.
Additionally, a digital inclusion impact assessment will be conducted, with recommendations to
ensure universal accessibility, including for elderly, minorities, and people with disabilities.
VI. Resilience and Extreme Scenarios ("Black Swan")
21. Fundamental Standard Vulnerability: IIF depends on open standards like W3C Verifiable
Credentials. What if a critical security vulnerability is discovered in the underlying standard itself,
compromising the integrity of all issued credentials? What would be the contingency plan for a
"zero-day vulnerability" at the heart of the protocol?
In case of critical vulnerability in standards like W3C Verifiable Credentials, the protocol provides
for:
• "Safe Version Rollback" emergency mechanism that temporarily disables verification of
new records until the standard is fixed.
• FISC technical committee activates Emergency Update Governance Layer mode with
accelerated voting by issuing members.
• Progressive re-issuance of compromised credentials with updated hashes and alerts to all
consuming platforms.
Additionally, IIF will require that every critical standard implementation undergo independent
third-party security audits with semi-annual frequency.
22. Audit Key Quorum: Protecting the audit key through MPC with a quorum of 3 parties is the
correct approach. But what if one of the participants in this quorum (for example, a large private
auditor) is secretly compromised by a sophisticated state actor? How would the system detect and
respond to an MPC participant acting in bad faith to try to force unauthorized access or reconstruct
the key?
The MPC-based quorum model with three parties includes additional safeguards:
• Periodic rotation of MPC operators, with revalidation every 3 months.
101

• Cross-checks (external watchdogs): anomalous behavior detection algorithms analyze
patterns of reconstruction or access attempts.
• Zero-knowledge (ZK) test for key use: all signatories must prove they received valid order
and real-time cryptographic authorization for legal key use.
If a participant is compromised, the quorum is immediately deactivated and migrated, and other
operators receive a security alert through parallel channel.
VII. Adoption and Interoperability with Legacy Systems
23. Integration "Last Mile": The scaling plan is clear. But what would be the estimated cost and
complexity for a large incumbent financial institution (a traditional bank) to integrate their decades-
old mainframe legacy systems, written in COBOL, with IIF's modern APIs? Are "connectors" or
"adapters" planned to facilitate this transition and reduce friction for major market players?
Integration with legacy systems, such as COBOL-based mainframes, can be complex and costly. IIF
provides for the creation of:
• Specific adapters (middleware) for traditional banks, with support for legacy protocols
(ISO 20022, SWIFT MT, etc.).
• SDKs with standardized libraries, developed in languages compatible with legacy systems
(Java, COBOL wrappers, etc.).
• Test environment (interoperability sandbox) to simulate real transactions with translation
layers between legacy systems and modern APIs.
Cost estimate: between $250 thousand to $2 million per institution, depending on complexity and
degree of obsolescence. Subsidies may be offered in partnership with regulators or public entities.
VIII. Ethics and Social Implications
24. Algorithmic Bias in Credentials: IIF allows portability of reputation. How does the system
ensure that algorithms used by entities to generate these credentials (e.g., "low-risk investor") don't
contain biases that discriminate, even unintentionally, against certain demographic groups? Who
audits the ethics of these issuance algorithms, and not just their technical security?
Issuing reputational credentials (e.g., risk score) can induce algorithmic bias. To mitigate this risk:
• Issuing entities will be required to publish and submit their models to bias and
algorithmic fairness audits, conducted by third parties.
• FISC maintains an Algorithmic Ethics Committee, with representatives from civil society,
academia, and regulators, to define minimum fairness standards.
• Credentials will be annotated with explanatory metadata about the algorithm used,
variables considered, and weightings applied, in an auditable manner.
This approach promotes algorithmic transparency and financial fairness, without giving up
automation and scalability.
25. Right to Contest and to be Forgotten: What is the formal process for an individual to contest
a credential they consider unfair, incorrect, or outdated? If an error in IIF harms someone's financial
102

reputation globally, what is the reparation mechanism and how quickly can it be activated to correct
the record across the entire network?
Individuals may contest a credential through a formal process integrated into the IIF protocol,
with the following steps:
• Digital request authenticated by the user in the wallet interface itself or issuer portal.
• Mandatory review by an impartial auditor within 7 business days.
• If the complaint is accepted, the credential can be revoked and re-issued, with automatic
notification to all network nodes.
• IIF also allows an "accelerated expiration" request, where an unfair credential loses
validity in up to 24 hours, while the dispute proceeds.
FISC will ensure that all corrections have complete propagation in up to 5 seconds, with visibility
to consuming platforms. This reduces the impact of compromised reputations and protects
individual rights.

Investment advisers following HOACP protocols and utilizing properly certified oracles could

Regulation A and Regulation D. However, safe harbor protection would not eliminate responsibility
for gross negligence, including ignoring evident oracle failure signs, failing to conduct minimum

Operational Mechanisms and Dispute Resolution
Oracle Divergence Resolution
Clear protocols address disagreements between oracles while maintaining operational efficiency.
Simple majority systems (2 of 3) approve or reject transactions. In case of ties or persistent
inconsistency, transactions receive marking for external auditor manual review, operations may face
temporary blocking through emergency protocols activation, and performance penalties may apply
to divergent oracles.
This ensures rapid execution without compromising integrity in volatile markets.
Transaction Finality versus Rollback
Programmable time-locks by value reduce irreversible movement risks. Transactions exceeding
$500,000 face 10-minute delays, while transactions exceeding $5 million face 30-minute delays.
Trade-offs include increased security enabling preventive action, with moderate liquidity impact
especially for institutional investors operating with planned windows. Whitelisting options for
previously audited addresses reduce delays while maintaining security.

During 24-hour resolution periods, assets face blocking via smart contracts with "under dispute"
status without transaction cancellation, only suspension. For opportunity loss responsibility,
successful client disputes may receive Reserve Fund coverage for real losses from suspension
through case-by-case analysis. Unsuccessful disputes result in client assumption of market risk.

Upgrade Key Governance
Multi-signature models include one SEC or designated SRO representative, one certified
independent auditor, and one rotating consortium of custodians and advisers (elected every 12
months). These three parties form a key governance committee with strict contract update rules,
ensuring transparency, monopoly absence, and impossibility of interested party capture.
Privacy Paradox in Complex Rules
Modular zero-knowledge circuits provide solutions with logical responsibility division. One oracle
validates portfolio data privately, while another validates concentration rules receiving only
